summary: This document summarizes the 2016 Internet of Things Software Update workshop held in Dublin. It records the discussion of requirements, challenges and possible solutions for delivering software and firmware updates to small connected devices.

eli5.summary: It is a report from a meeting where experts talked about how to safely give tiny smart gadgets their software fixes.

subtitle: Expert findings on securely updating software on small networked devices.

tldr.problem: IoT devices must stay online for years and receive security fixes, but small devices have severe constraints on power, memory, and connectivity, and there are no agreed standards for how to deliver and verify updates safely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes a 2016 workshop where experts in IoT, security, and standards discussed requirements, challenges, and solutions for firmware updates, considering device classes, signing keys, dependencies, and deployment scenarios.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified gaps in standardized update mechanisms and recommended that the standards community develop reference implementations and best practices to help device makers build secure, maintainable update systems.

sections.title: The IoT Update Challenge
sections.content:
IoT devices—from smart home gadgets to industrial sensors—are expected to run for 10 or more years with Internet connectivity. When vulnerabilities are discovered, they need security fixes. However, unlike desktop computers and smartphones (which can download and install updates from app stores), IoT devices are often constrained: they have limited RAM and storage, no operating system's built-in package manager, and sometimes unstable connections. Implementing a robust software update mechanism for these devices is non-trivial and expensive, so many devices ship without one.

The RFC reports on an Internet Architecture Board workshop held in June 2016 in Dublin where experts from device vendors, security researchers, standards bodies, and operators came together to discuss the state of the art and identify what standards and best practices the industry needs. The workshop explored protocol mechanisms, security, metadata formats, privacy implications, and the role of device ownership and control.
sections.eli5: Small internet-connected devices need security updates to stay safe, but they are too limited to use the update systems that phones and computers use. Nobody had yet agreed on how to do it right.

sections.title: Key Requirements and Questions
sections.content:
Workshop participants identified several critical requirements. Data origin authentication (proving that an update comes from the right source) was deemed essential—without it, an update becomes a vulnerability. Devices must be able to verify signatures on updates, though not all low-end devices currently support asymmetric cryptography. The mechanism must handle dependencies between software components and know about the device's hardware and configuration. Partial updates (sending only changed parts rather than full images) could reduce bandwidth, but only if the device can handle reassembly.

Questions emerged about multiple signatures (should an OEM sign, then an enterprise, then a regulator?), key rollover (how to update signing keys over a device's long lifetime), and multiple owners (who authorizes updates on a shared device?). The group recognized that different device classes—from A-class (like a Raspberry Pi running Linux) to M-class (tiny microcontrollers)—need different approaches.
sections.eli5: Everyone agreed: updates must prove who they come from, must work on tiny devices, must handle upgrades to the signing keys, and must not break existing devices. But it was unclear exactly how.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Challenges
sections.content:
Beyond technical requirements, the workshop discussed practical deployment issues. Incentives across the value chain are misaligned: a device maker might not see enough benefit to justify implementing updates, and once a device is sold, the original maker might have no incentive to provide updates for years. An end-of-support scenario raises the question: when a vendor stops supporting a device, who should be allowed to provide updates (a successor company, an open-source community, the device owner themselves)?

The workshop also explored mesh networks (where devices relay updates to each other), compromised devices (how to handle a device that has been hacked), and measurements and analysis (how to know if an update rollout is working). The discussion revealed that while more powerful IoT devices can use mechanisms similar to desktop software updates (like package managers), constrained devices often must use firmware updates (entire binary images) from specific vendors, with little infrastructure to ease the process.
sections.eli5: The makers of devices do not always want to support them for 10 years. Devices often cannot talk to each other to pass along updates. And once a device is hacked, it is hard to fix it if the maker is gone.

sections.title: Gaps and Next Steps
sections.content:
The workshop concluded that there is a real risk IoT devices will continue to be shipped without solid update mechanisms. The group recommended that the standards community (particularly the IETF) develop standardized mechanisms tailored to constrained devices, with public documentation and reference implementations. Instead of requiring a single mechanism to fit all device classes, the recommendations suggested supporting multiple mechanisms (firmware images for M-class, package managers for A-class) with common security building blocks.

Most of the workshop notes raise questions rather than definitive answers. However, the shared recognition that secure updates are essential, combined with the detailed enumeration of constraints and scenarios, provided a foundation for future standardization efforts. The report emphasizes that device makers need standardized, well-reviewed mechanisms to choose from, not proprietary ad-hoc solutions.
sections.eli5: The group decided that the standards community should create a toolkit and guidelines so that device makers can build good update systems instead of making them up.
